title: How to Sit With Someone Who Is Suffering
excerpt: The instinct is to fix, to explain, to make the pain smaller so we can stand it. Almost everything that helps requires us to do less and stay longer.
body:
When someone we love is suffering, our first move is usually for ourselves. We rush to say something, anything, because the silence is unbearable to us, and so we fill it with explanations and reassurances and verses we have not earned the right to quote yet. We tell ourselves we are helping. Mostly we are managing our own discomfort, and the suffering person can feel the difference. They can tell when you are present with them and when you are present with your need to feel useful.

Job's friends are the cautionary tale. For seven days they sat with him in the dust and said nothing, and that was the best thing they ever did. Then they opened their mouths, and everything went wrong. They explained his suffering. They built theology on top of his wounds. By the end God rebukes them, not Job. The lesson is hard and clear. Presence blessed him. Explanation harmed him.

## Show up before you know what to say

The most common reason people stay away from the suffering is that they do not know what to say. So learn this first: you do not need to know what to say. You need to come. Knock on the door. Send the text that does not require a reply. Sit in the hospital chair. Your presence says what no sentence can, that this person is not alone, that their pain has not made them untouchable. Waiting for the perfect words is just a respectable way of not showing up.

## Stop trying to fix it

Most suffering cannot be fixed, and the suffering person already knows this better than you do. When you reach for a solution, you are subtly telling them their pain is a problem you can solve, which means it is also a problem they should already have solved. Resist the fix. Resist the silver lining. Resist "have you tried." Your job is not to end their suffering. Your job is to refuse to let them go through it by themselves.

## Ask, then listen, then stay quiet

Ask what this is like for them. Then listen without preparing your response. When they finish, do not rush to fill the gap. Let the silence sit. Some of the most healing moments are wordless, two people in a room, one in pain and one unwilling to leave. If you must speak, reflect back what you heard rather than adding your own commentary. "That sounds unbearable" does more than a paragraph of advice.

## Do not borrow their grief and make it yours

There is a way of caring that turns the focus back on the helper, where you weep so hard the suffering person ends up comforting you. Feel it, yes. But carry your own reaction so they do not have to. The room belongs to their pain, not yours.

## Bring the practical, not just the spiritual

Love has hands. Drop off food without asking what they need, because they cannot answer. Mow the lawn. Take the kids for an afternoon. Sit with the patient so the caregiver can sleep. Suffering is exhausting in the most ordinary ways, and the casserole on the porch preaches a sermon the words cannot. Do not say "let me know if you need anything." They will not. Just do the next obvious thing.

## Stay past the funeral

Everyone comes the first week. The casseroles stop, the cards stop, and that is precisely when the loneliness arrives, when the rest of the world has moved on and the suffering has not. Mark your calendar for week six, month three, the first anniversary. Show up when no one else does. That is when your presence means the most, and it costs you the most, which is the point.

**This week:** Think of one person you have been avoiding because you did not know what to say. Stop avoiding. Send a short message that asks nothing of them: "I have been thinking about you. You do not need to reply. I am here." Then put a reminder in your phone to reach out again in three weeks.

We were not made to suffer alone, and the deepest thing we can offer one another is not an answer but a body in the next chair, unwilling to leave. You will say the wrong thing sometimes. Say it, and stay anyway. The staying is the love.
